title: Théorie arithmétique. Théorie de Galois des motifs (1965) : notes manuscites (s.d.), tapuscrit (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Context: this page is part of Grothendieck's sketch of a 'Galois theory of motives'. G is the motivic Galois group (Tannakian fundamental group) of a category of motives. G^0 is its identity component. ε and μ are extra structures; on this page ε appears to be the Tate (cyclotomic) character G→G_m. j is the weight cocharacter (weight grading). Pol(G) is the set of polarizations.

(1) Bracketed question. Does the automorphism group of (G^0_R, ε_R, μ_R), or of (G^0_#, ε, μ), or of (G, ε, μ), act transitively on Pol(G)? Equivalently, is it impossible to single out a privileged polarization, or a privileged class of polarizations?

(2) Test case: geometric motives over F_q, q = p^n. Assume Tate/semisimplicity, so that G^0 is a pro-torus whose character group M is a group of Weil q-numbers inside a CM field L (L totally imaginary quadratic over a totally real K). Grothendieck observes that there is a distinguished conjugacy class of cocharacters i: G_{m,C} → G_C. On a character λ ∈ M it is given by λ ↦ (1/n)·v_𝔭(λ), where 𝔭 is a prime of L (in fact of Q̄) above p. Thus i is the p-adic slope (Newton) cocharacter.

He checks the identity ī·i = j. Complex conjugation exchanges 𝔭 and 𝔭̄, and λλ̄ = q^{w(λ)}, so v_𝔭(λ) + v_𝔭(λ̄) = weight. He also checks ε∘i = id: the Tate motive has eigenvalue q, of slope 1. So i is a characteristic-p analogue of the Hodge cocharacter μ_Hodge, which satisfies μ·μ̄ = weight.

To pin i down one must 'normalize' G_C by a choice of i. This requires choosing an algebraic closure Q̄ and a p-adic place. The margin notes that i is well defined up to Q̄-conjugation.

He then claims:
- an automorphism of G^0 respecting i is the identity;
- the effectivity structure on M is determined by i; effective motives are those with all slopes ≥ 0, i.e. Frobenius eigenvalues that are algebraic integers;
- effectivity on the M_K (K a field related to R?), in particular on M_R and M_C, is determined by the system of conjugates of i.

The idea seems to be that this rigidifying datum might also make a polarization canonical, answering (1) in the finite-field case.

The circled marginal boxes are only partly legible:
- the formula is to be understood via (p-adic) absolute values;
- a worked example appears: L = Q(√−p), q = p ≠ 2, i.e. the supersingular-type Weil number √−p, of slope 1/2, with some congruence condition on p (3, 7, 11 mod something).

The neighbouring pages are an unrelated typed English text on projective embeddings.
errors: The formula λ ↦ (1/n)v_𝔭(λ) gives a homomorphism M → Q, not M → Z (e.g. slope 1/2 for √−p). So i is only a fractional (Q-)cocharacter, an element of Hom(G_m,G)⊗Q, i.e. a Newton-type cocharacter. It is not a genuine homomorphism G_m → G_C as written, unless one passes to a cover of G_m.

Normalization inconsistency: the bracket writes v_𝔭(q) = 1 but also divides by n. Only one normalization (v(p) = 1 with the 1/n factor, or v(q) = 1 without it) is consistent. Ramification of p in L must also be accounted for.

The claim 'an automorphism of G^0 respecting i is the identity' seems false as stated. Automorphisms of the Weil-number torus induced by the decomposition group D_𝔭 ⊂ Gal(Q̄/Q) preserve v_𝔭, hence i. For example, with L = Q(√−p), λ ↦ λ̄ preserves the slopes. At best rigidity holds modulo such automorphisms or with extra structure.
i is naturally defined over Q̄ (indeed via a p-adic place), not just over C. Its conjugacy class depends on the Galois orbit of the place, which the margin partly acknowledges.

ideas.what: Over F_q the motivic Galois group (assuming Tate) is a pro-torus whose characters are Weil q-numbers in CM fields
ideas.modern_name: Weil-number protorus P / motivic Galois group of motives over finite fields
ideas.usually_credited_to: Langlands–Rapoport 1987; Milne 1994 ('Motives over finite fields'); Saavedra Rivano 1972 (partial)

ideas.what: Distinguished (fractional) cocharacter of the motivic Galois group defined by p-adic valuations of Frobenius eigenvalues at a chosen place above p
ideas.modern_name: slope / Newton cocharacter (Langlands–Rapoport cocharacter of the pseudomotivic groupoid; Kottwitz's Newton point)

ideas.what: Identity ī·i = weight, ε∘i = id: the slope cocharacter as characteristic-p analogue of the Hodge cocharacter (μμ̄ = weight)
ideas.modern_name: Newton cocharacter as p-adic analogue of Hodge cocharacter; Shimura–Taniyama formula linking slopes and CM types
ideas.usually_credited_to: Shimura–Taniyama (slopes of CM reductions), Langlands–Rapoport, Milne

ideas.what: Effectivity of motives over F_q read off Tannakianly from the Galois conjugates of the slope cocharacter (all slopes ≥ 0 ⇔ integral eigenvalues)
ideas.modern_name: effective Weil numbers / integrality (Honda–Tate) expressed via cocharacters
ideas.usually_credited_to: Honda–Tate (integrality); Tannakian phrasing implicit in Milne

ideas.what: Question whether automorphisms of (G, ε, μ) act transitively on polarizations, or whether a privileged polarization exists
ideas.modern_name: uniqueness/canonicity of polarizations in Tannakian categories; Hodge standard conjecture over finite fields
ideas.usually_credited_to: Saavedra Rivano 1972; Deligne–Milne 1982; Milne 2002 ('Polarizations and Grothendieck's standard conjectures')
ideas.where_published: Grothendieck's 'Standard conjectures' (1969) discusses positivity but not this Tannakian question

missed.claim: Grothendieck (notes dated 1965, possibly later) singles out the p-adic slope cocharacter of the motivic Galois group of motives over F_q, with ī·i = weight and ε∘i = id. He notes that its normalization requires a choice of Q̄ and a place above p. This is essentially the cocharacter used by Langlands–Rapoport (1987) and Milne in defining the pseudomotivic groupoid, conceived two decades earlier.
missed.quote: il y a une classe de conjugaison d'homomorphismes i : G_{m,C} → G_C distinguée, avec ī i = j, ε i = id ... par la formule (1/n) v_p(λ)
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is historical priority for a key ingredient of the Langlands–Rapoport conjecture and of motives over finite fields. It also shows Grothendieck explicitly viewed slopes as the char-p replacement for the Hodge cocharacter.

missed.claim: He proposes using the slope cocharacter to rigidify the motivic Galois group and to determine effectivity (and implicitly a canonical polarization) for motives over finite fields, answering whether a privileged polarization exists. This program is close in spirit to Milne's later work on canonical polarizations over F_q via CM lifting, but is phrased purely Tannakianly.
missed.quote: La structure d'effectivité sur M est déterminée grâce à i ... par la connaissance des systèmes des conjugués
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: A Tannakian characterization of effectivity and polarizations over F_q via slope cocharacters could feed into current work on the Hodge standard conjecture in characteristic p and on Tate-class formalisms.

deep.surprise_reason: The page anticipates, in Tannakian language, the slope/Newton cocharacter of the Weil-number torus and its role as a Hodge-cocharacter analogue (μμ̄ = weight). That is usually attributed to Langlands–Rapoport and Milne in the 1980s–90s. The idea is sketchy, contains a fractional-cocharacter gap and a dubious rigidity claim, and the underlying facts (Shimura–Taniyama slopes, Honda–Tate) were partly known. So the surprise is notable but moderate.
transcription_corrections: Margin 'Hom (G_m, G^0_C)' is likely 'Hom(G_m, G^0_C)' in context 'i est bien défini à conjugaison près par Q̄ (?)'; the rest is illegible.
'v_p(λ) v_p(λ̄) = v_p(λλ̄)' should read as a sum: v_𝔭(λ) + v_𝔭(λ̄) = v_𝔭(λλ̄) (written multiplicatively/by juxtaposition in the manuscript). Also 'p' here denotes a prime ideal 𝔭 of L above p.
'j^*(λ)' is probably 'j(λ)' (the weight of λ); 'v_p(q)=1' as written.
In the box, 'J=0' is uncertain; the example L = Q(√−p), q = p ≠ 2 suggests a weight-1, slope-1/2 Weil number rather than j = 0.
